text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended slightly weaker in quiet trade. May lost 40 cents to close at $306.0 per tonne, while August closed 20 cents lower at $305.70 per tonne. Raw sugar futures in New York remained within their recent trading range in a thinly traded session. May lost 5 points to close at 10.81 cents/lb, while July gave up 3 points close at 10.60 cents/lb. The outer months lost between 3 and 6 points.

Cyclone Justin, which hit the Australian cane crop, will have no impact on overall production. According to trade sources the cyclone caused a loss of 250,000 tonnes of sugar but that will be offset by better growing conditions following heavy rains. Without fresh offtake or any other fundamental news, prices must be expected to remain within their current trading range.

AUSTRALIA - Damage caused by cyclone Justin over the weekend might not have been as bad as initially thought. According to trade sources, the amount of sugar lost in the worst affected areas could amount to roughly 250,000 tonnes, raw value, or around 5 per cent of overall production.

However, as Justin on its fringes brought much needed rain to other growing areas sugar production there might even have got a boost. This might result in a rise in sugar output by over 200,000 tonnes. Hence the production outlook for Australia in 1997/98 is likely to remain unchanged.

BELGIUM - Sugar beet sowings are behind those of last year. Up to March 26 1,565 ha have been sown out of a total area planned of 102,586 ha (1.53 per cent). At the same stage last year a total of around 6 per cent of the overall area had been drilled.

SAUDI ARABIA - According to press reports the Al-Jouf Agriculture Development Co., a Saudi Arabian agricultural company, has received government approval to build the kingdom's second sugar refinery with an annual production capacity of 120,000 tonnes of white sugar and 42,000 tonnes of molasses.

Total investment was put at 335 mn Riyals, 50 per cent of which will be financed by the Saudi Industrial Development Fund (SIDF). However, it is not known when construction and commercial production will begin. The first refinery built by the United Sugar Company, recently commenced operations in Jeddah.

This has an initial capacity of 500,000 tonnes but with the option of increasing it to 630,000 tonnes. The USC refinery is 51 per cent owned by Savola - Saudi Arabia's biggest food group, 15 per cent by Britain's Tate & Lyle Plc. and the rest by Saudi sugar refining firms. The erection of a second sugar refinery in Saudi Arabia will make the country mainly a raw sugar importer, a hard blow for white sugar exporters.

CAMEROON - Sugar production in Cameroon in 1996/97 (December/November) is estimated at 48,000 tonnes, white value, down from 52,000 tonnes produced the previous year. Sugar consumption in 1996/97 is estimated to rise to 90,000 tonnes, up from 85,000 tonnes in 1995/96. These figures suggest that the country will have to import more than in previous years.

BARBADOS - Sugar production in Barbados in 1998 is forecast to reach 67,000 tonnes, raw value, up from 62,000 tonnes expected for 1997 and 59,114 tonnes produced in 1996. Consumption is expected to remain stable at 15,000 tonnes.
